title: 22. Interview: LFU (Least Frequently Used)
summary: Interview Q&A for LFU (Least Frequently Used) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 LFU (Least Frequently Used) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is LFU, and how does it differ from LRU?
**Answer:** LFU (Least Frequently Used) is a cache eviction policy that removes the entry with the lowest access count when the cache is full. The intuition is frequency: a key accessed many times is more likely to be accessed again than a key accessed once, regardless of when the last access was. LFU differs from LRU in its signal: LRU uses **recency** (when was the last access?) while LFU uses **frequency** (how many accesses total?). LFU wins on stable-hot-set workloads (the hot set's high counts protect it) and on scan-heavy workloads (one-time scans don't accumulate enough count to evict high-frequency keys). LRU wins on temporal-locality workloads (recently accessed = likely re-accessed) and on shifting-hot-set workloads (LRU adapts within a few cache-misses; LFU adapts slowly because old counts persist). LFU's weakness is slow adaptation: a key that was hot yesterday but cold today keeps its high count, occupying space that should go to new hot keys. Mitigations include frequency aging (Redis's `lfu-decay-time`) and sketch resets (W-TinyLFU). Real-world: Redis 4.0+ offers `allkeys-lfu`; Caffeine's W-TinyLFU uses a Count-Min Sketch for frequency estimation with aging.
**Visual:**
```
LRU signal:  recency (when was the last access?)
             + adapts fast to hot-set shifts
             + good for temporal-locality (sessions)
             - NOT scan-resistant (scans wipe hot set)

LFU signal:  frequency (how many accesses total?)
             + scan-resistant (low-count scans don't evict high-count hot)
             + good for stable hot sets (popular products)
             - slow adaptation (old counts persist, zombies stay)
             - mitigated by aging (Redis lfu-decay-time, W-TinyLFU sketch reset)
```

### Q2. What data structures support an efficient LFU cache?
**Answer:** Three common approaches: (1) **Min-heap** (priority queue) keyed by access count: get is O(log n) (increment count, sift up), put is O(log n) (evict min, insert), eviction is O(log n) (pop min). Simple but slower than LRU's O(1). Often used with lazy deletion (mark old heap entries invalid, skip them on pop) to avoid O(n) re-heapify on every count update. (2) **Frequency buckets**: a hashmap from count to a set (or OrderedDict) of keys with that count, plus a `min_freq` pointer. Get is O(1) (move key from bucket N to bucket N+1, advance `min_freq` if bucket N is empty). Put is O(1) (evict an arbitrary/LRU key from the `min_freq` bucket, insert the new key in bucket 1). This is the production-grade approach. (3) **Count-Min Sketch** (W-TinyLFU): a probabilistic data structure with sub-byte counters; estimates frequency with O(1) updates and minimal memory (~10 bytes per entry). The sketch is aged periodically to allow adaptation. Redis's `allkeys-lfu` uses 8-bit saturating counters with probabilistic increment (counter increments with probability `1 / (counter * lfu-log-factor + 1)`) and decay by 1 every `lfu-decay-time` minutes — a memory-efficient approximate LFU. Caffeine's W-TinyLFU uses a Count-Min Sketch with periodic aging.
**Visual:**
```
Min-heap LFU (O(log n)):
  heap: [(1,K4),(2,K2),(5,K1),(100,K3),(5000,K5)]
  evict: pop min -> (1,K4)
  get(K1): increment count, push new entry, lazy-delete old

Frequency-bucket LFU (O(1)):
  count=1:    {K4}            <- min_freq=1, evict from here
  count=2:    {K2}
  count=5:    {K1}
  count=100:  {K3}
  count=5000: {K5}
  get(K1): move K1 from bucket 5 to bucket 6

Count-Min Sketch LFU (W-TinyLFU):
  + sub-byte counters, O(1) update
  + aged periodically (reset / halve) for adaptation
  + ~10 bytes per entry overhead
```

### Q3. Why is LFU scan-resistant, and why is this important?
**Answer:** LFU is scan-resistant because a one-time scan read gives the scanned key an access count of 1 (or 0 in a sketch), which is far below the counts of the hot working set (hundreds or thousands). When the cache is full and LFU must evict, it evicts the lowest-count entries first — the scanned keys — preserving the high-count hot keys. This is the opposite of LRU, where each scan read makes the scanned key "more recently used" than the hot keys, evicting them. Scan resistance is important because real-world caches routinely see scans: nightly backups reading every key, periodic crawls (search engines, monitoring), batch analytics jobs, and cache warm-up scripts. Without scan resistance, a single scan can wipe the hot working set and collapse hit rate from 95% to 0% until the hot keys are re-loaded. Example: a Redis cache with `allkeys-lru` and a 1000-key hot set at 95% hit rate; a nightly backup scans 100,000 keys; after the scan, the cache holds the last 1000 scanned keys (all cold); hit rate drops to 0% until the hot keys are re-accessed. Switching to `allkeys-lfu` preserves the hot set: scanned keys (count = 1) are evicted before hot keys (count = thousands); hit rate stays at 95% during the backup. Real-world: Amazon's product catalog cache uses LFU-like policies because crawls are frequent; Redis operators switch to `allkeys-lfu` when they discover backup-scan pollution.
**Visual:**
```
Scan of 100 cold keys, hot key K5 has count=5000:

LRU (NOT scan-resistant):
  each scan read makes the scanned key "most recently used"
  -> hot keys evicted to admit scanned keys
  -> after scan: cache full of cold data, hit rate 0%

LFU (scan-resistant):
  each scan read gives the scanned key count=1
  -> hot key K5 (count=5000) never evicted by count=1 scans
  -> after scan: hot set still resident, hit rate 95%

Importance:
  + backups, crawls, batch jobs are routine in production
  + without scan resistance, hit rate collapses during scans
  + LFU / W-TinyLFU preserve the hot working set
```

### Q4. What is LFU's slow-adaptation weakness, and how is it mitigated?
**Answer:** Pure LFU never decrements counts, so a key that was hot (count = 10,000) but is now cold (no accesses) keeps its high count forever — occupying space that should go to new hot keys. The cache fills with "zombie" entries that were once hot but are now dead. Example: a viral video's metadata cached at count = 100,000; the video stops trending; the metadata stays in the cache forever (no entry has a higher count to evict it); the cache wastes space on dead data while new viral videos can't get cached. Mitigations: (1) **Frequency aging** — periodically decay all counts (e.g., halve them every hour, or decrement by 1 every N minutes). Redis's `lfu-decay-time` does this: every `lfu-decay-time` minutes, the counter is decremented by 1, so a key with count 1000 and no accesses decays to 0 in 1000 × `lfu-decay-time` minutes. (2) **Windowed frequency** — track frequency only over a recent window (e.g., last 1 hour of accesses), not lifetime count. Caffeine's Count-Min Sketch is periodically reset (or halved) to achieve this. (3) **Segmented LFU** — keep a "recent" segment and a "frequent" segment; new admissions go to recent, and only after accumulating count are promoted to frequent; this prevents one-time accesses from polluting frequent and allows the recent segment to act as an adaptation buffer. (4) **W-TinyLFU** — combines all three (windowed sketch + segmented spaces + admission control) and is the modern state of the art. Real-world: Redis's `lfu-decay-time` defaults to 1 minute; Caffeine's W-TinyLFU ages the sketch periodically.
**Visual:**
```
Pure LFU (no aging):
  K_viral: count=100,000 (was hot, now cold)
  K_new_hot: count=5 (newly hot)
  + K_viral never evicted (no entry has higher count)
  + K_new_hot can't displace K_viral
  + cache wasted on zombie K_viral

With aging (Redis lfu-decay-time=1 min):
  T=0:      K_viral count=100,000
  T=1min:   K_viral count=99,999  (decayed)
  T=100K min: K_viral count=0    (fully decayed)
  + K_new_hot eventually displaces K_viral

W-TinyLFU (sketch reset + segmented):
  + sketch periodically halved -> old freqs decay
  + window LRU captures new hot keys by recency
  + admission control promotes only high-freq to main
```

### Q5. How does Redis implement approximate LFU, and what are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** Redis 4.0+ implements `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu` using **8-bit saturating counters with probabilistic increment and periodic decay**. Each key's counter is 8 bits (max 255). On access, the counter increments with probability `1 / (counter * lfu-log-factor + 1)` — so a counter at 0 always increments, but a counter at 100 increments with probability ~1/101, slowing growth logarithmically. This lets an 8-bit counter effectively represent frequencies up to millions of accesses (saturating at 255 only after extreme use). Decay: every `lfu-decay-time` minutes (default 1), the counter is decremented by 1, allowing old hot keys to lose priority over time. Eviction: like approximate LRU, Redis samples N keys (`maxmemory-samples`, default 5) and evicts the one with the lowest counter. Trade-offs: (1) **Memory efficiency** — 8 bits per entry is negligible overhead, vs 16+ bits for a true count. (2) **Approximation error** — the probabilistic increment and sampling introduce ~5% hit-rate deviation from true LFU. (3) **Tuning knobs** — `lfu-log-factor` (default 10) controls how fast counters grow (higher = slower growth, more discrimination among high-frequency keys); `lfu-decay-time` controls aging rate. (4) **No per-key recency within a frequency** — ties in counter are broken arbitrarily (no LRU-within-frequency), unlike the textbook frequency-bucket LFU. Real-world: Redis's LFU is documented in `redis.conf` with extensive comments; operators tune `lfu-log-factor` based on workload access rates.
**Visual:**
```
Redis approximate LFU:
  + 8-bit counter per key (max 255)
  + probabilistic increment: P(increment) = 1/(counter*lfu_log_factor + 1)
      counter=0:    P=1.0   (always increment)
      counter=100:  P=1/101 (~1%)
      counter=255:  saturated
  + decay: counter -= 1 every lfu_decay_time minutes (default 1)
  + eviction: sample N=5 keys, evict lowest counter

Trade-offs:
  + memory: 8 bits/entry (negligible)
  + ~5% hit-rate deviation from true LFU
  + tuning: lfu_log_factor (counter growth rate)
            lfu_decay_time (aging rate)
  + no LRU-within-frequency (ties broken arbitrarily)
```

### Q6. What is W-TinyLFU, and why is it considered the state of the art?
**Answer:** W-TinyLFU is a modern eviction policy that combines a small windowed LRU (1% of capacity, for recency) with a main space governed by TinyLFU admission control (80% probationary, 20% protected, for frequency). When the window LRU fills and a candidate must be promoted to the main space, TinyLFU compares the candidate's estimated frequency (from a Count-Min Sketch) against the victim's frequency; the candidate is admitted only if higher. The Count-Min Sketch uses sub-byte counters and is periodically aged (halved) to allow adaptation. W-TinyLFU is state of the art because: (1) **Scan-resistant** — one-time scans have low sketch frequency, rejected at admission. (2) **Adapts to shifts** — the aged sketch forgets old frequencies, so previously-hot keys lose priority. (3) **Captures recency** — the window LRU handles bursty short-term patterns and new hot keys. (4) **Achieves hit rates within 1% of the theoretical optimum (Belady's MIN)** on most workloads. (5) **Low overhead** — the sketch adds ~10 bytes per entry, negligible vs the value size. Caffeine (used by Netflix, Uber, Spring Boot) defaults to W-TinyLFU; Hazelcast and Apache Ignite also use it. Redis 4.0+'s `allkeys-lfu` is inspired by similar ideas (frequency with aging) but uses sampling rather than a sketch. Real-world: Caffeine's benchmarks show W-TinyLFU outperforming LRU and LFU by 5–30% on real-world traces, especially scan-heavy ones.
**Visual:**
```
W-TinyLFU layout:
  +----------------+------------+---------------+
  | Window LRU 1%  | Probation  | Protected 20% |
  | (recency)      | 80%        | (frequency)   |
  +----------------+------------+---------------+

New key -> Window LRU (always admitted)
  when window full -> candidate for main space
  TinyLFU admission:
    if candidate_freq > victim_freq (from Count-Min Sketch):
      admit candidate, evict victim
    else:
      reject candidate, keep victim

Sketch: Count-Min Sketch with sub-byte counters, periodically aged (halved)

Why state of the art:
  + scan-resistant (low-freq scans rejected)
  + adapts to shifts (aged sketch forgets old freqs)
  + captures recency (window LRU)
  + within 1% of Belady's MIN (theoretical optimum)
  + low overhead (~10 bytes/entry)
```

### Q7. When would you choose LFU over LRU, and when is LFU wrong?
**Answer:** Choose LFU when: (1) **The workload is scan-heavy** — backups, crawls, batch jobs routinely read every key; LFU's scan resistance preserves the hot set; LRU would be wiped. (2) **The hot set is stable** — popular products, trending videos, top-N entities; frequency is a strong predictor. (3) **The workload is Zipf-distributed with a long tail** — a small set of keys dominates accesses; LFU's frequency tracking protects them. (4) **You can use aging or W-TinyLFU** — pure LFU's slow adaptation is mitigated by frequency decay (Redis's `lfu-decay-time`) or sketch resets (W-TinyLFU). LFU is wrong when: (1) **The hot set shifts frequently** — LFU adapts slowly; LRU's recency signal is stronger for shifting hot sets (sessions, recently-viewed lists). (2) **The workload is pure temporal-locality** — recently accessed keys are likely to be re-accessed, but no key is accessed many times; LFU's frequency signal is weak (everyone has count 1). (3) **Implementation simplicity matters** — pure LFU is more complex than LRU (min-heap or frequency buckets vs hashmap + linked list); for in-process caches where simplicity is paramount, LRU is the safer default. (4) **Pure LFU without aging** — old hot keys become zombies; you must use aging or W-TinyLFU. Real-world: Redis recommends `allkeys-lru` for general workloads, `allkeys-lfu` for stable hot keys with scans; Caffeine defaults to W-TinyLFU (combining both).
**Visual:**
```
Choose LFU when:                   Avoid LFU when:
  + scan-heavy (backups, crawls)     + shifting hot set (sessions)
  + stable hot set (popular items)   + pure temporal locality
  + Zipf with long tail              + simplicity matters (LRU is simpler)
  + with aging or W-TinyLFU          + pure LFU without aging (zombies)

Workload                  Best policy
------------------------  ------------------------------
scan-heavy + stable hot   LFU or W-TinyLFU
stable hot, no scans      LFU (slight edge over LRU)
shifting hot, no scans    LRU (adapts fast)
temporal locality         LRU
mixed (real-world)        W-TinyLFU (best of both)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your Redis cache uses `allkeys-lru` and has 95% hit rate. After nightly backups, hit rate drops to 50% for 30 minutes. What's happening, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The nightly backup is causing **scan pollution**: the backup sequentially reads every key, and Redis's `allkeys-lru` treats each scanned key as "recently used," evicting the hot working set to admit cold backup-scanned keys. After the backup, the cache is full of cold data, and the next wave of normal traffic misses the hot keys, dropping hit rate to 50% until the hot keys are re-loaded (which takes 30 minutes as traffic gradually repopulates the cache). Fix: **switch to `allkeys-lfu`** (`CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu`). LFU is scan-resistant — the backup-scanned keys have count = 1 (or low in the sketch), while the hot working set has count = thousands; LFU evicts the scanned keys before the hot keys, preserving the hot set during the backup. Expected outcome: hit rate stays at 95% during backups, drops to ~93% briefly (the backup itself loads some keys), recovers immediately after. Alternative fixes: (1) Backup from a read-replica of the database instead of the cache (avoids polluting the cache entirely). (2) Use Redis's `SCAN` with `NOTOUCH` flag (available in Redis 6.0+) to scan without updating recency — preserves LRU's hot set without switching to LFU. (3) Throttle the backup (slow it down so the cache can absorb), but this doesn't fix the underlying pollution. The best fix depends on the architecture: if the cache is the source of truth, switch to LFU; if the DB is the source, back up from a replica. Real-world: many Redis operators discover LFU specifically because of backup-scan pollution.
**Visual:**
```
Nightly backup with allkeys-lru:
  backup scans 1M keys -> each marked "recently used"
  -> hot working set evicted
  -> after backup: cache full of cold data
  -> hit rate: 50% (until hot set re-loaded, ~30 min)

Fix: CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu
  + backup-scanned keys have count=1 (low)
  + hot working set has count=thousands (high)
  + LFU evicts scanned keys before hot keys
  -> hit rate stays 95% during backup

Alternative:
  + backup from DB read-replica (don't touch cache)
  + Redis SCAN with NOTOUCH (6.0+) - scan without recency update
```

### Q2. Your product catalog cache has 10M products, with the top 1000 products accounting for 50% of traffic. A search engine crawler periodically scans all 10M products. Which eviction policy minimizes DB load?
**Answer:** This is a textbook case for **LFU or W-TinyLFU**. The top 1000 products are stable and high-frequency (50% of traffic); the crawler scan reads all 10M products periodically (one-time reads, low frequency). With LRU, the crawler scan would wipe the top 1000 from the cache (each scanned product becomes "more recently used" than the hot products), dropping hit rate to near 0% during and after the crawl. With LFU or W-TinyLFU, the crawler-scanned products have frequency 1 (or low in the sketch), while the top 1000 have frequency thousands; LFU evicts the scanned products before the hot products, preserving the top 1000 throughout the crawl. Expected hit rate with LFU: ~50% (hot set stays resident) + ~5% (long-tail hits, since the cache can hold 10M of 10M products — wait, the cache is sized at... let's assume the cache holds 1M products, 10% of the catalog). With cache size 1M: hot 1000 stay resident (50% of traffic hits cache); long-tail of 9.999M products with 50% of traffic — cache holds ~1M of them (10% of long tail), so long-tail hit rate is ~5% (10% × 50% adjusted for skew). Total: ~55% with LFU. With LRU during a crawl: ~5% (hot set wiped, only long-tail-in-cache hits). The 50-point difference is dramatic — LFU reduces DB load by ~10x compared to LRU on this workload. Real-world: Amazon, eBay, and other large catalogs use LFU-like policies precisely because of crawler scans.
**Visual:**
```
Workload:
  + 10M products, cache holds 1M (10%)
  + top 1000: 50% of traffic (stable, high freq)
  + crawler: scans all 10M periodically (one-time, low freq)

LRU during crawl:
  + each scanned product is "most recently used"
  + top 1000 evicted by the scan
  + hit rate during/after crawl: ~5% (only long-tail-in-cache hits)

LFU during crawl:
  + scanned products have count=1 (low)
  + top 1000 have count=thousands (high)
  + scanned products evicted before top 1000
  + hit rate during crawl: ~55% (hot set preserved)

DB load reduction: ~10x (LFU vs LRU on this workload)
```

### Q3. You're using Redis with `allkeys-lfu` and `lfu-decay-time=1` (default). A viral video goes from 0 to 1M views/hour overnight, then back to 0 the next day. How does the cache behave, and what tuning would help?
**Answer:** Behavior with defaults: (1) **During the viral spike** — the video's counter rapidly saturates (8-bit counter with probabilistic increment reaches 255 after ~10K accesses with `lfu-log-factor=10`); the video is admitted to the cache and stays at the top of the frequency ranking; hit rate for the video is ~100% (always cached). (2) **After the spike** — the video gets no more accesses; with `lfu-decay-time=1`, the counter decrements by 1 every minute; from 255, it takes 255 minutes (~4 hours) to decay to 0; during those 4 hours, the video occupies cache space that should go to new hot videos. (3) **The next viral video** — its counter starts at 0 and grows; until it exceeds the first video's decayed counter (which takes hours), the first video stays resident and the new video may be evicted. Tuning to help: (1) **Decrease `lfu-decay-time`** — e.g., to 0.1 (6 seconds); the counter decays 10x faster, so the first video's counter reaches 0 in ~25 minutes instead of 4 hours; the cache adapts to the shift faster. (2) **Increase `lfu-log-factor`** — e.g., to 20; the counter grows slower, so it saturates at a higher access count; this gives more discrimination among high-frequency keys but doesn't help with adaptation. (3) **Switch to W-TinyLFU (Caffeine)** — if the cache is in-process; W-TinyLFU's sketch is aged (halved) periodically, giving faster adaptation than Redis's linear decay. The trade-off of faster decay: less frequency signal for genuinely stable hot keys (a key accessed 100/hour but with fast decay might decay below a new key accessed 50/hour, causing unnecessary eviction). Real-world: TikTok and Twitter tune LFU decay for viral content; the right decay rate depends on the typical hot-key lifetime.
**Visual:**
```
Viral video lifecycle with lfu-decay-time=1 (default):
  T=0:      counter=0, video not cached
  T=1hr:    counter=255 (saturated), video cached, hit rate 100%
  T=2hr:    spike ends, no more accesses
  T=2hr+:   counter decays -1/min
  T=6hr:    counter=0 (4 hours to decay from 255)
  + for 4 hours, video occupies space despite being dead

Tuning: lfu-decay-time=0.1 (6 seconds)
  + counter decays 10x faster
  + video reaches counter=0 in ~25 minutes (not 4 hours)
  + new viral video admitted faster

Trade-off: faster decay = less signal for stable hot keys
  (a key accessed 100/hr might decay below a new key accessed 50/hr)
```

### Q4. Your team is using pure LFU (no aging) for a news article cache. After a month, hit rate has dropped from 90% to 60%, even though traffic is the same. What's happening?
**Answer:** Pure LFU without aging has **slow adaptation** — old hot keys keep their high counts forever, even after they're no longer accessed. Over a month, the cache has accumulated "zombie" entries: news articles that were hot in week 1 (high count) but are now cold (no accesses). These zombies occupy cache space that should go to new hot articles (week 4's trending news). The cache fills with old news, and new hot articles can't displace them (new articles have low counts, old zombies have high counts). Hit rate drops because the cache holds dead data instead of the current hot set. Fixes: (1) **Add frequency aging** — periodically decay all counts (e.g., halve every day, or decrement by 1 every minute); this allows zombies to lose priority as new hot articles accumulate count. In Redis, set `lfu-decay-time` to a small value (e.g., 60 minutes) so old articles decay within a day. (2) **Switch to W-TinyLFU** — Caffeine's W-TinyLFU ages the sketch periodically, adapting to shifts. (3) **Use a TTL** — set a TTL on news articles (e.g., 7 days) so old articles are evicted regardless of count; this is a coarse but effective fix for news (which has natural expiration). (4) **Reset counts periodically** — every week, halve all counts (a coarse aging); this is a poor man's frequency decay. (5) **Combine LFU with TTL** — LFU for eviction order, TTL for hard expiration; this is the most robust for news. Real-world: news sites (CNN, BBC, NYT) typically use TTL + LFU; articles expire after 24–48 hours, and LFU orders eviction within the TTL window. The lesson: pure LFU without aging is brittle on workloads with shifting hot sets; always add aging or TTL.
**Visual:**
```
Pure LFU on news articles (no aging):
  Week 1: article A goes viral, count=100,000 (cached, hot)
  Week 2: article B goes viral, count=100,000 (cached, hot)
  Week 3: article C goes viral, count=100,000 (cached, hot)
  Week 4: article D goes viral, count=5,000 (new, lower count)

  + A, B, C all have count=100,000 (zombies, no longer accessed)
  + D has count=5,000 (current hot)
  + LFU evicts D before A/B/C (D has lowest count)
  + cache fills with zombies, hit rate drops 90% -> 60%

Fix: add aging (lfu-decay-time=60min)
  + A/B/C counts decay over time
  + D's count grows with current accesses
  + D eventually exceeds A/B/C's decayed counts
  + D stays resident, zombies evicted
  + hit rate recovers to 90%
```

### Q5. You're using Caffeine (W-TinyLFU) for an in-process cache. Hit rate is 92%, but you've noticed it drops to 70% during a marketing campaign with a flood of new users. Why, and what do you do?
**Answer:** The marketing campaign drives a flood of accesses to **new keys** (new user profiles, new product pages) that aren't yet in the cache's frequency sketch. W-TinyLFU's admission control compares the candidate's frequency (from the Count-Min Sketch) against the victim's frequency; new keys have frequency 0 (or 1 after first access), so they're rejected at admission in favor of existing entries with higher frequency. This is usually good (scan-resistant), but during a campaign, the new keys are *legitimately* hot — they should be admitted — but W-TinyLFU's conservative admission rejects them, dropping hit rate. Fixes: (1) **Increase the window LRU size** — Caffeine exposes this; a larger window admits more new entries based on recency alone, before frequency-based admission kicks in. (2) **Pre-warm the cache** — when a campaign starts, pre-load the new hot keys (e.g., from a list of campaign products) so they bypass the admission filter. (3) **Increase the cache capacity during campaigns** — auto-scale the cache size to absorb the burst; the frequency sketch will catch up as accesses accumulate. (4) **Accept the temporary drop** — 70% is still acceptable; once the campaign stabilizes, the new keys accumulate frequency and hit rate recovers to 92%. (5) **Use a higher sketch reset frequency** — age the sketch faster so new keys can build up frequency quicker (at the cost of less discrimination for stable hot keys). Real-world: Netflix pre-warms caches for new show launches; Amazon pre-warms product caches for Prime Day. The lesson: W-TinyLFU's strength (scan resistance) is also its weakness when the "scan" is actually legitimate new traffic.
**Visual:**
```
Normal operation:
  + hot keys have high freq in sketch -> admitted on eviction
  + new keys have low freq -> rejected (scan resistance)
  + hit rate: 92%

Marketing campaign (flood of new users):
  + new keys are legitimately hot but have low freq
  + W-TinyLFU rejects them (treats as scan)
  + hit rate: 70% (new keys can't get admitted)

Fixes:
  + pre-warm cache with campaign keys (bypass admission)
  + increase window LRU size (more recency-based admission)
  + auto-scale capacity during campaigns
  + accept temporary drop (recovers as freq accumulates)
  + faster sketch aging (new keys build freq quicker)
```

### Q6. You're building a WhatsApp message cache. Each user's recent messages are accessed frequently (within the chat view), but messages older than 24 hours are rarely accessed. Which eviction policy do you choose?
**Answer:** This is a workload with **temporal locality (recent messages are hot) plus a hard expiration (24-hour useful life)**. The best policy is **LRU with a TTL of 24–48 hours** — not LFU. Reasoning: (1) Messages are accessed frequently within the first hour (the user is in the chat), then access drops to near-zero after 24 hours. This is temporal-locality, which LRU captures well (recent messages stay at the head of the recency list). (2) LFU would be wrong — most messages have similar access counts (1–5 accesses within the chat view); LFU's frequency signal is weak (no key is accessed thousands of times), and the access counts don't differentiate hot from cold well. (3) A TTL of 24–48 hours handles the hard expiration: messages older than the TTL are evicted regardless of policy, freeing space for new messages. (4) Within the TTL window, LRU keeps the most recently accessed messages (the user's active chats) resident. (5) The combination (LRU + TTL) is the standard pattern for chat caches. For Redis: `maxmemory-policy volatile-lru` (LRU among TTL'd keys) with `EXPIRE` set to 24–48 hours per message. For Caffeine: `expireAfterWrite(24, HOURS)` with the default W-TinyLFU eviction (W-TinyLFU is fine here; the TTL handles expiration). Real-world: WhatsApp, Telegram, and Signal use TTL + recency-based caches for messages; old messages are evicted by TTL, recent messages by LRU when capacity is exceeded. The lesson: match the policy to the access pattern — temporal-locality + hard expiration → LRU + TTL, not LFU.
**Visual:**
```
WhatsApp message access pattern:
  + recent messages (last 1 hour): accessed frequently (chat view)
  + 1-24 hour messages: accessed rarely (scroll-back)
  + >24 hour messages: almost never (archived)

Best policy: LRU + TTL(24-48h)
  + LRU: recent messages stay resident (temporal locality)
  + TTL: old messages auto-evicted (hard expiration)
  + LFU would be wrong: similar access counts, weak signal

Redis: maxmemory-policy volatile-lru + EXPIRE per message
Caffeine: expireAfterWrite(24h) + W-TinyLFU (TTL handles expiration)

Lesson: temporal-locality + hard expiration -> LRU + TTL, not LFU
```

### Q7. Your team is debating LFU vs W-TinyLFU for a Redis cache. W-TinyLFU isn't natively available in Redis. What do you recommend, and why?
**Answer:** Redis doesn't natively offer W-TinyLFU (it offers `allkeys-lru`, `allkeys-lfu`, `allkeys-random`, and `volatile-*` variants). For most workloads, **Redis's `allkeys-lfu` with appropriate `lfu-decay-time` and `lfu-log-factor` tuning** is the closest approximation to W-TinyLFU and is the right choice for scan-heavy or stable-hot-set workloads. Reasoning: (1) Redis's LFU includes frequency aging (`lfu-decay-time`), which addresses pure LFU's slow-adaptation weakness — the main benefit of W-TinyLFU's sketch aging. (2) Redis's LFU uses sampling (`maxmemory-samples`), which is approximate but avoids the lock contention of a true global LFU — similar to W-TinyLFU's non-blocking design philosophy. (3) Redis's LFU doesn't have W-TinyLFU's window LRU (recency capture) or admission control (candidate-vs-victim frequency comparison), so it's less scan-resistant than true W-TinyLFU — but for most workloads, the difference is small (~2–3% hit rate). (4) If true W-TinyLFU is essential (e.g., the workload is extremely scan-heavy and Redis's LFU isn't good enough), consider: (a) using an in-process Caffeine cache in front of Redis (Caffeine handles the hot set with W-TinyLFU, Redis handles the larger warm set with LRU or LFU); (b) using a Redis module or fork that adds W-TinyLFU (non-standard, maintenance burden); (c) moving to a different cache (Hazelcast, Apache Ignite) that supports W-TinyLFU natively. Recommendation: start with Redis's `allkeys-lfu` with `lfu-decay-time=1` (default) and `lfu-log-factor=10` (default); measure hit rate; if it's below your SLO, consider adding a Caffeine layer in front. Real-world: Netflix uses Caffeine (in-process, W-TinyLFU) in front of Redis (LFU) for tiered caching — the best of both worlds.
**Visual:**
```
Redis doesn't offer W-TinyLFU natively. Options:

1. Redis allkeys-lfu (recommended for most workloads):
   + frequency with aging (lfu-decay-time)
   + sampling-based (no lock contention)
   + ~2-3% below true W-TinyLFU hit rate
   + tuning: lfu-decay-time, lfu-log-factor, maxmemory-samples

2. Caffeine (in-process) in front of Redis:
   + Caffeine: W-TinyLFU for hot set (sub-us reads)
   + Redis:    LFU/LRU for warm set (network reads)
   + tiered caching, best of both worlds
   + used by Netflix, Uber

3. Switch to Hazelcast/Apache Ignite (W-TinyLFU native):
   + only if Redis LFU is insufficient AND Caffeine layer isn't viable
   + high migration cost

Recommendation: start with Redis allkeys-lfu + tuning;
                add Caffeine layer if hit rate below SLO.
```

quiz.explanation: LFU (Least Frequently Used) is a cache eviction policy that removes the entry with the lowest access count when the cache is full. The intuition is frequency: a key accessed many times is more likely to be accessed again than a key accessed once, regardless of when the last access was. LFU differs from LRU in its signal: LRU uses recency (when was the last access?) while LFU uses frequency (how many accesses total?).

quiz.explanation: Redis 4.0+ implements maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu using 8-bit saturating counters with probabilistic increment and periodic decay. Each key's counter is 8 bits (max 255). On access, the counter increments with probability 1 / (counter * lfu-log-factor + 1) — so a counter at 0 always increments, but a counter at 100 increments with probability ~1/101, slowing growth logarithmically.
